query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium, lightweight Mg‐containing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) produced by rapid solidification, the initially supersaturated solid solution gradually decomposes during controlled annealing into a two‐phase microstructure—a soft matrix interspersed with uniformly distributed nanoscale intermetallic precipitates—that acts as a precursor for selective oxidation. These precipitates, enriched in reactive species (e.g. Mg- and Cu- or other element–rich intermetallics), preferentially oxidize at high temperatures to form a dual-layer, more protective oxide film and equilibrate local electrochemical potentials during corrosion. This microstructural evolution thereby reduces the corrosion current density and improves high-temperature oxidation resistance compared with the as-cast metastable state.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, metastable, Mg-containing lightweight HEA (e.g. an Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd based alloy) with a predominantly solid solution microstructure and sparse, incoherent intermetallic precursors, and an overall density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Applying a controlled annealing (heat treatment) schedule designed to induce diffusion‐driven precipitation without complete equilibration, thereby promoting the nucleation and uniform dispersion of nanoscale intermetallic phases.
generation.conditions: The heat treatment should be performed at an intermediate temperature (e.g. 300–500 °C) for a defined duration under inert atmosphere, followed by exposure to high-temperature oxidation conditions (400–600 °C in controlled oxygen partial pressures) and electrochemical corrosion testing (e.g. in 0.1 M NaCl solution) at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoscale intermetallic precipitates that develop from the metastable solid solution act as structural mediators by locally altering oxidation kinetics and modulating galvanic coupling during corrosion.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates have a higher affinity for oxygen than the surrounding matrix, so during oxidation they form discrete, adherent oxide nodules that coalesce into a protective dual-layer film. Concurrently, in corrosive environments, the spatial variation in composition provided by these precipitates reduces micro-galvanic disparities, leading to a more uniform passivating film formation and lower anodic dissolution rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast metastable baseline, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit: (1) a dual-layer oxide scale with an inner passivating layer derived from the oxidized intermetallics, (2) lower corrosion current densities and more positive corrosion potentials when measured electrochemically, and (3) enhanced oxidation resistance as evidenced by reduced mass gain in thermogravimetric analysis at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly solidified metastable solid solution state without significant intermetallic precipitation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to operate for Mg-containing HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ processed under non-equilibrium conditions, and in environments where the heat treatment can trigger controlled nano-precipitation without full coarsening (i.e. avoiding temperatures and durations that allow complete equilibrium phase formation).
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends findings from PMC7579168::web::035::5_conclusions (which describe diffusion-driven precipitation in non-equilibrium processing) and PMC12299034::web::007::1_introduction/PMC12299034::web::000::abstract (which correlate specific intermetallic phase formation with improved passivation and corrosion resistance in Mg–Ti–Zn alloys), by applying a similar mechanistic framework to a different Mg-containing lightweight HEA. The uncertainty lies in the exact nature, size, and distribution of the precipitates in the new alloy system, and how these details control the selective oxidation behavior; these parameters are not yet fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one group remains in the as-cast state (metastable SS) and the second is subjected to the controlled annealing treatment designed to induce nanoscale intermetallic precipitation. Characterize the microstructures using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD); then perform high-temperature oxidation tests (thermogravimetric analysis under controlled oxygen atmosphere) and electrochemical corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization in 0.1 M NaCl).
measurements: Quantitative phase analysis (volume fraction, size distribution) via TEM/XRD
Oxide scale morphology and composition via XPS or SEM-EDS
Corrosion current density and corrosion potential from polarization curves
Mass gain kinetics from TGA during oxidation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant formation of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates, or if there is no observable improvement in oxide film protective quality (i.e. similar or higher corrosion current densities and oxidation rates) compared to the as-cast samples, then the proposed mechanism linking microstructural evolution with enhanced corrosion and oxidation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRecently, the design of lightweight high entropy alloys (HEAs) with a mass density lower than 5 g/cm3 has attracted much research interest in structural materials. We applied a first principles-based high-throughput method to design lightweight HEAs in single solid-solution phase. Three lightweight quinary HEA families were studied: AlBeMgTiLi, AlBeMgTiSi and AlBeMgTiCu. By comprehensively exploring their entire compositional spaces, we identified the most promising compositions according to the following design criteria: the highest stability, lowest mass density, largest elastic modulus and specific stiffness, along with highest Pugh’s ratio. We found that HEAs with the topmost compositions exhibit a negative formation energy, a low density and high specific Young’s modulus, but a low Pugh’s ratio. Importantly, we show that the most stable composition, Al0.31Be0.15Mg0.14Ti0.05Si0.35 is energetically more stable than its metallic compounds and it significantly outperforms the current lightweight engineering alloys such as the 7075 Al alloy. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.

The selected Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 and Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 alloys were analysed for structural behavior by CALPHAD, solidification and kinetics simulations. Phase diagrams showed the formation of a multiphase structure with preponderant solid solutions. Intermetallic compound-based phases were found at lower concentrations but still significantly higher than in the conventional aluminum alloys. Two invariant transformations were indicated for Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, with a BCC-A2 phase stable between 316–488 °C. The influence of the elements on the structural evolution were similar with the results obtained from semiempirical criteria calculations. The non-equilibrium solidification simulation discussed the order of which the phases are solidifying in normal casting conditions. The soft FCC phase is stabilizing first in the Al3.4Cu0.5Si0.2Zn0.5Mg0.2 alloy, while intermetallic compound phases Mg2Si and Al9Mn2Si are forming first in the Al3Mn0.2Zn0.3Mg0.7Si0.8 alloy.
